title: Chapter 4 Teaching Competency Development
venue: Handbook of Teaching Competency Development in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This chapter addresses the problem of how to systematically develop teaching competencies in higher education. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, it proposes a broad framework for competency development and reviews how different actors and systems contribute to teacher development at international, governmental, societal, institutional, and individual levels. The chapter frames teaching competency as a complex capability shaped by policy, resources, training opportunities, professional norms, and teachers’ motivation.

The approach discussed is a conceptual and policy-oriented framework, not an empirical study. It outlines action goals, action subjects, action objects, action content, action methods, and action evaluation for teaching competency development. Examples include courses, seminars, workshops, consultation, teaching awards, evaluation systems, digital teaching resources, and teacher development centers. The chapter also highlights digital tools and artificial intelligence in teacher development, including AI-assisted teacher team-building pilots in China and digital platforms for teacher training, resource sharing, diagnosis, and evaluation.

The population focus is higher education teachers, including pre-service, new, and in-service teachers, across universities and related institutions. The context is primarily higher education in China, with additional examples from UNESCO, the United States, the United Kingdom, Finland, Brazil, and other international settings. The main conclusion is that improving teaching competency requires coordinated support across policy, institutions, society, and individual practice, with increasing emphasis on digital platforms, ICT competencies, and AI-enabled support systems for training, evaluation, and professional growth.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a handbook chapter and policy/framework discussion with no original empirical design, control group, or quantitative analysis. It provides examples and recommendations rather than evaluative evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The chapter describes potentially important institutional uses of AI in teacher development, but it does not demonstrate measured impact. Any benefits are asserted qualitatively, so impact is unclear rather than evidenced.

interventions.use_case: A policy and framework chapter describing how AI is integrated into higher-education teacher development initiatives, including AI-assisted teacher team building, intelligent assistants for teachers, smart classrooms, intelligent education/literacy training, and teacher big-data/evaluation systems.

finding.finding_summary: This is a framework and policy chapter, not an empirical evaluation, so it does not report causal effects or effect sizes. It synthesizes how institutions, governments, and international organizations implement teacher-competency development, including AI-enabled teacher training pilots, digital platforms, and evaluation systems.
finding.measure: Policy/program descriptions; implementation examples; no quantitative outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that AI-supported platforms and teacher big-data systems can reduce teacher burden, improve homework design and evaluation, and support more efficient teacher management and diagnosis. These claims are descriptive rather than empirically tested, and no effect sizes or sample sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, homework design/evaluation capacity, and administrative efficiency (descriptive only)
